extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; educated laypeople and medical/natural history enthusiasts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on recognizing the clinical stages, epidemiology, prognosis, and basic treatment principles for yellow fever, aimed at informed lay and medical readers. The page also contains a separate natural-history discussion giving anatomical criteria to distinguish birds from reptiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical onset and prodromal symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: An attack of yellow fever is generally quite sudden, though in some cases there are slight premonitory symptoms such as loss of appetite, general uneasiness, headache, or costiveness. It is commonly ushered in by chilliness alternating with flushes of heat, or the person may be overcome with languor and extreme debility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These early, often non-specific signs may be followed quickly by high fever (temperature often reaching 102°F in a few hours). Be alert to sudden changes from mild prodrome to full disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic first-stage clinical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Fever accompanied by headache (often over the eyes or shooting temple-to-temple), severe loin pains, full strong rapid pulse (90–120/min), hot dry skin, flushed face, bloodshot watery eyes, and tongue with creamy white fur but red tip and edges. Early stomach uneasiness leads in 12–24 hours to nausea and persistent vomiting; intense thirst; bowels initially costive, then becoming loose as disease progresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation of the constellation (fever, headache, severe loin pain, vomiting, intense thirst, characteristic tongue) supports early clinical identification; patient often debilitated yet restless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course and stages including deceptive lull
rubrics_metrics.description: Fever intense for two or three days (often worse in the evening, temp sometimes 104–105°F), then subsides and may return nearly to normal within twelve hours; on third or fourth day yellow discoloration of skin appears. In many cases this lull is deceitful and followed by the gravest stage with small thready pulse (30–40/min), returning nausea and vomiting, dry brown tongue, cool dry skin, hiccough, apathy or delirium/stupor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinicians must not assume improvement during an apparent remission—closer monitoring is required as severe deterioration may follow quickly (black vomit, hemorrhages, urine suppression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Black vomit and late-stage systemic disorganization as fatal signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Disorganization of blood and tissues leads to bleeding into stomach; vomited blood altered by gastric acids forms 'black-vomit' varying from brown to jet black (coffee-grounds appearance). Urine may be scanty or suppressed, or black and bloody. Increasing skin discoloration (dusky brown, livid, or mahogany), frequent hemorrhages (mouth, nose, eyes, subcutaneous), cadaverous odor, convulsions or coma may lead to death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of black vomit generally indicates profound systemic damage and is usually fatal. Monitor for haemorrhages and renal suppression as grave prognostic signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible variability of symptoms and atypical presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Symptoms vary greatly across times, localities, and individuals; some patients may fall into collapse and die within hours, others may be ambulatory and insist they are well, and classic signs like jaundice or black vomit can occur in other diseases or be absent in yellow fever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a single sign; use a combination of clinical findings and context (epidemic setting, exposure history) to identify cases. Consider differential diagnoses and coexisting morbid processes (e.g., malarial fevers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration, relapses, and mortality range
rubrics_metrics.description: The disease lasts from three to nine days and recovery in severe cases may be slow. Relapses are uncommon. The mortality varies between five and seventy-five percent of those attacked, depending on outbreak and local factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect wide variability in outcomes; historical mortality rates differ greatly by epidemic and locality—use caution when extrapolating to current settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incubation period and susceptible populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Disease develops in from one to fourteen days after exposure. Those most liable are strangers or recent comers; old residents often enjoy some immunity except in severe epidemics. Some occupational exposures (tanners, butchers, soap-boilers, scavengers) seem almost exempt, while trades exposing to great temperature variation (bakers, cooks) are more prone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure history (recent arrival/travel, occupational environment) is important. Note that immunity after infection is generally lifelong though reinfection may rarely occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epidemiological/climatic requirements for outbreaks
rubrics_metrics.description: To become epidemic, yellow fever requires a mean temperature of at least 72°F (some argue as high as 80°F for extended periods); it follows water-courses and lines of ocean-travel, appearing in commercial port cities and beginning at the wharves. It rarely occurs inland, is uncommon in elevated regions (commonly regarded as limited above ~2,500 feet), and disappears entirely at freezing temperatures (32°F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health vigilance should focus on warm, moist port areas and low elevations during warm seasons; temperature drops abate epidemics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission character: fomites and nidus requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Yellow fever occupies a position between contagious and non-contagious diseases: the poison is not directly communicable like smallpox; however, emanations of the sick are connected with spread but seem to require an appropriate warm, moist nidus in which germs can germinate and develop. Germs are portable and may be conveyed in baggage or merchandise (fomites) for long distances. If not so conveyed, progress is slow and puzzling (e.g., moving about a few feet a day, skipping houses/blocks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control measures should consider fomite transmission and environmental nidus elimination; unpredictable patterns of spread require careful local investigation of sanitation and storage of materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal treatment measures
rubrics_metrics.description: All methods agree on principal points: clear the bowels at the start; keep the patient perfectly quiet; keep temperature down by applications of cold water and ice (ice to head if signs of brain congestion); relieve excessive thirst with lumps of ice; control nausea with iced lemonade or champagne; lemon-juice used externally in West Indies; caution with premature return to solid food when appetite revives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatment is largely supportive and symptomatic. Avoid premature feeding; use cooling and careful gastric/nausea management. Note regional folk practices (e.g., lemon-juice rubbing) are observed but should be contextualized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of favorable termination (crisis signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Favorable termination indicated by gradual amelioration of symptoms or sometimes by profuse perspiration, sudden cessation of nausea, rapid return of pulse to natural fullness and strength, or other marked events suggesting a crisis in the disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor for these turning points as positive prognostic signs; their absence or reversal suggests progression to severe disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/geographical notes on outbreaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Yellow fever first fully recorded outbreak in West Indies in 1647; epidemics have occurred as far north as Quebec and as far south as Montevideo; endemic areas include West Indies, Venezuela, New Granada, Mexico, and parts of U.S. coastlines (as far north as Charleston, S.C.). New Orleans historically had repeated epidemics with widely varying death tolls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding historical patterns helps contextualize risk; port cities and trade routes are recurrently implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of feathers and beak (avian defining characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Birds may be characterized generally as feathered bipeds whose mouth is modified into a beak encased in a horny sheath, sometimes serrated, but never presenting true teeth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feathers and a toothless horny beak are primary external criteria to classify an animal as a bird.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winged forelimbs and flight-related skeletal adaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: Fore-limbs assume the form of wings more or less developed; skeleton shows adaptations such as a high crest (keel) on the center of the breastbone for attachment of wing muscles; collar-bones unite to form the 'merry-thought' (furcula); forelimb bones are pneumatized (air passages into hollow shafts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of these osteological features (keeled sternum, fused clavicles, pneumatic bones) supports avian identification and adaptation to flight; absence or modification (e.g., in flightless birds) must be interpreted in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avian hindlimb and pelvic specializations (ploughshare bone, hock pulley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bird haunch-bone (pelvis) consolidated into one element with margins free and separated beneath; instead of a tail the posterior spinal segments form a 'ploughshare' bone supporting tail quills; leg (tibia) shows a prominent ridge or crest on the front of its upper extremity; fibula slender and attached only at upper end; hock-bone lower end formed into a triple (trifid) pulley-shaped articulation for toes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These combined pelvic and hindlimb characteristics are diagnostic of birds and distinguish them from reptiles whose pelvis remains in two halves and whose limb bones retain different articulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pneumatized skull and bones and air-sac extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: In birds the hollow shafts of stronger bones contain small pores (air-passages) by which air-sacs (extensions of lung air-tubes) are prolonged into the bones; the skull also contains numerous air-cavities (though filled from nasal/ear chambers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bone pneumatization is a distinctive physiological/anatomical avian trait linked to respiration and flight; its presence in fossils/osteological remains supports avian affinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm-bloodedness and absence of true teeth
rubrics_metrics.description: Every one who has handled a living bird knows it is warm-blooded; birds have no true teeth (beak instead), whereas many reptiles possess strong sharp teeth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thermoregulatory physiology and dentition are functional characters supporting classification, but fossil inference on warm-bloodedness is indirect—use with other anatomical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reptile defining characters (scaly skin, ectothermy, dentition, limb configuration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reptiles' bodies are protected by modifications of skin into scales, horny plates, or shields; they are cold-blooded due to circulatory peculiarities (mixing aerated and unaerated blood), most possess two pairs of legs with fore- and hind-limbs similar, and typically possess powerful jaws set with strong sharp teeth. Tails are generally elongated and terminal segments do not unite into a ploughshare bone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These external and internal traits distinguish reptiles from birds; when present, they argue for reptilian affinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reptilian osteological contrasts (unfused pelvic halves, distinct fibula, multiple hock bones)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reptiles the 'collar-bones' do not unite to form a furcula; the breastbone does not develop a median keel; fibula is well-developed parallel to tibia throughout length; hock has at least four distinct bones articulating as many toes; haunch-bone composed of two halves articulating with the spine but not united beneath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These osteological differences are key for fossil classification: absence of avian fusion patterns and presence of multiple separate elements favor reptilian identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embryonic ossification centers and lifelong unfused ossicles in reptiles
rubrics_metrics.description: All bones in embryonic condition are cartilaginous with ossification centers forming as animals mature; among higher animals centers become indistinct with age, but among many reptiles bones either continue throughout life with component parts unsolidified or indicate lines of union, making it easy to tell their composite parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent separate ossification centers and visible union lines in bones are indicative of reptilian affinity; in fossils, such markers help distinguish reptile vs. bird.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions when fossils show mixed avian and reptilian characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Fossil examples (e.g., Ichthyornis, Hesperornis) may show a mosaic of characters—some strongly avian (keeled breastbone, united clavicles, wing bones) and some reptilian (biconcave vertebrae, separate pelvic elements). Such mixed traits complicate classification and demand careful comparative osteological analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution: weigh the preponderance and functional significance of characters (e.g., adaptations for swimming) and avoid overreliance on a single trait. Comparative context with living and extinct taxa is essential.
